source_read: PMC HTML, PMC10630900 (publisher's version, JAMA 2023;330(17):1653-1665), read in full in my own browser tab: key points, abstract, introduction, methods, results with the Table, discussion, applicability, limitations, conclusions, article notes (funding, conflicts, role of funder) and references. The forest plots (Figures 2, 4, 5 and 6) are images only; I viewed them enlarged and summed their counts. Figure 7 (harms summary) and Supplements 1-2 (eTables 1-5, eAppendix) were not read. I also read the linked correction notice (PMC11447627, JAMA 2024;332(16):1397): it corrects only an author's middle initial (Mark J. Edlund), not any data.

claims.overstatement: None. 'Is associated with' matches the review's own wording, and 'most of them European and most after detoxification' matches its account: of 23 acamprosate studies, 16 were European, and most trials required some days of abstinence first. The review's figures behind this are inconsistent: the Results give 23 acamprosate studies (16 European, 4 US), the Discussion 5 US trials and '15 of 22' trials elsewhere recruiting from inpatient settings.
claims.note: Every McPheeters number in the claim matches the Table and text: return to any drinking RR 0.88 (0.83-0.93), 20 trials, 6380, moderate; I² 77.64% (Figure 2: tau² 0.01, Q(19) 84.97, P < .001); return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94-1.05), 7 trials, n 2496, moderate (no effect); percentage of drinking days WMD -8.3 (-12.2 to -4.4), 14 trials, 4916; diarrhoea RR 1.58 (1.27-1.97); head to head with naltrexone, return to any drinking 1.03 (0.96-1.10), 3 trials, 800. Internal inconsistencies, which do not change the direction: (1) Figure 2's 20 trials sum to 5931 analysed participants (2326/3115 vs 2319/2816, 74.7% vs 82.4%), not the Table's 6380. Its COMBINE-like row (16 weeks, 244/303 vs 254/309) is labelled 'Anton et al, ref 17, 2005', but ref 17 is a naltrexone trial; Figure 5 labels the same 303 vs 309 groups 'Anton et al, ref 19, 2006' (COMBINE). (2) Figure 5 (return to heavy drinking) plots 11 comparisons and pools RR 1.00 (0.96-1.04), I² 0%. The four head-to-head trials (COMBINE, Kiefer 2003, Morley 2006, Mann 2013) each appear twice, three of them with the identical acamprosate arm. The seven first rows sum to exactly 2496, the Table's n for 0.99 (0.94-1.05). The four second rows sum to exactly 1141, the n of the acamprosate-vs-naltrexone pool, and their comparator columns hold the naltrexone arms (e.g. Mann 169, Morley 53). So Figure 5 appears to pool head-to-head comparisons with naltrexone as if they were placebo-controlled, entering acamprosate arms twice. The claim correctly uses the Table's estimate. The Discussion attributes the lack of benefit in the US acamprosate trials to recruitment by advertisement and more varied drinking, against inpatient recruitment elsewhere, which supports the claim's account. 'The three reviews share most of their trials': 81 of McPheeters' 118 RCTs came from the 2014 review. Funding: AHRQ contract 75Q80120D00007 (task order 75Q80122F32004); AHRQ gave technical assistance but did not take part in the searches, eligibility, analysis or approval; conflicts: none reported.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement. Small points: (1) 'Disulfiram did not reduce return to any drinking' reads as a firm null. The review says only that the 3 trials did not show an association, graded low (no effect), so 'showed no clear difference' fits better. (2) The Results text contradicts the gabapentin figure the claim uses. It says gabapentin was not significantly associated with reduced return to heavy drinking, while giving RR 0.90 (0.82-0.98), an interval that excludes 1. The Table and Discussion treat it as low-strength evidence of benefit, as the claim does; the inconsistency is worth a word. (3) 'Mostly with a psychosocial co-intervention' holds whichever of the review's figures is used (87 of 118, 73.7%, or 100 of 118 with any co-intervention).
claims.note: Every number checked against the Table and the Results text. Topiramate: percentage of drinking days WMD -7.2 (-14.3 to -0.1), 8 trials, 1080; heavy drinking days -6.2 (-10.9 to -1.4), 9 trials, 1210; drinks per drinking day -2.0 (-3.1 to -1.0), 7 trials, 922; all moderate. Topiramate harms: paraesthesia RR 3.08 (2.11-4.49), taste 3.01 (1.70-5.34), cognitive dysfunction 2.37 (1.58-3.55). Baclofen: return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.70-0.98), 8 trials, 995, low (of 13 baclofen RCTs, 1607 people); drowsiness 1.46 (1.15-1.86), dizziness 1.89 (1.40-2.55), sleepiness 1.81 (1.11-2.97); deaths 8 vs 3 (4 trials, 660), insufficient. Gabapentin: return to heavy drinking 0.90 (0.82-0.98); return to any drinking 0.92 (0.83-1.02); 3 trials, 522, low; cognitive dysfunction 2.76 (1.51-5.06), dizziness 1.70 (1.24-2.32). Disulfiram: 1.03 (0.90-1.17), 3 trials, 622, low (no effect). Injectable naltrexone: return to any drinking 0.96 (0.90-1.03), 2 trials, 939; return to heavy drinking 1.00 (0.82-1.21), 2 trials, 615; low (no effect). The P values printed beside each pooled estimate are unlabelled and cannot be effect tests: for example, baclofen 0.70-0.98 with P < .001, and injectable naltrexone drinking days with an interval excluding 0 and P = .23. They are most likely heterogeneity tests. Injectable naltrexone drinking days: the abstract and text give WMD -4.99 (-9.49 to -0.49), the Table prints -9.49 to 0.49, and the abstract calls it days over 30 days rather than a percentage; the claim does not use this. Disulfiram: the Discussion notes 4 further small RCTs excluded for design. The supervision point in the claim is attributed to Jonas 2014 and is not in this paper. Funding and conflicts as in the acamprosate claim.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the McPheeters figures. 'Reduced return to heavy drinking' is causal, while the review says 'associated with'. It is acceptable for double-blind RCT evidence of moderate strength, which is the claim's certainty. Two qualifiers: (1) The harms the claim cites (nausea, dizziness, vomiting) were assessed for all naltrexone doses together, not for the tablets at the usual dose alone. (2) 'Effects in people still drinking ... are uncertain' is fair, but the review notes 3 studies in people not yet abstinent that reported less heavy drinking with naltrexone or acamprosate.
claims.note: Numbers checked against the Table and Figures 4 and 6. Return to heavy drinking (oral, usual dose): RR 0.81 (0.72-0.90), 23 trials, 3170, moderate; Figure 6 lists 23 trials, I² 58.72%, and sums to 3172 by my reading. Return to any drinking: 0.93 (0.87-0.99), moderate. Percentage of drinking days -5.1 (-7.16 to -3.04), 15 trials. Heavy drinking days -4.3 (-7.60 to -0.91), 7 trials. Any dose, return to heavy drinking 0.86 (0.80-0.93), 27 trials, 4645. Higher oral dose 0.93 (0.84-1.01), 2 trials; injection 1.00 (0.82-1.21), 2 trials; both low (no effect). Nausea 1.73 (1.51-1.98), dizziness 1.99 (1.47-2.69), vomiting 1.53 (1.23-1.91). Head to head 1.03 (0.96-1.10) and 1.02 (0.93-1.11), 4 trials, 1141. Deaths 1 vs 2 (6 trials, 1738), insufficient. Inconsistencies in the source the claim inherits: (1) For return to any drinking, the Table and text give 16 trials and n 2347 (the 2014 review's counts), but Figure 4's usual-dose subgroup lists 20 trials summing to 2719 (Q(19), I² 35.07%). 2719 is exactly the any-dose total of 4604 minus the higher-dose (946) and injection (939) subgroups, and 20 + 3 + 2 = 25 matches the any-dose count. So the claim's '16 trials, 2347' (magnitude) should read 20 trials, 2719, or be flagged. (2) For return to heavy drinking, the Results text gives the NNT with 19 trials and n 2875 (again the 2014 counts), against 23 and 3170 in the Table and Figure 6. (3) The printed NNT intervals do not follow from the RR intervals: 11 (5-41) for heavy drinking against 7.5-20.9 implied, and 18 (4-32) for any drinking against 9.7-126 (editors' calculation). The claim does not use them. 'More than half of the people in one US trial' is not stated in the text, which names the four trials only as refs 19 (COMBINE, US), 37 (Kiefer 2003), 45 (Mann 2013) and 48 (Morley 2006). But it can be derived. The four repeated second rows of Figure 5 are COMBINE 303+309, Kiefer 40+40, Morley 55+53 and Mann 172+169, summing to exactly 1141, the head-to-head n. COMBINE therefore supplies 612 of 1141 (53.6%, editors' calculation), so 'more than half' holds. Applicability: participants' mean age was typically 40-49; 63 of the 70 studies reporting race and sex were majority White men; most participants likely had moderate to severe disorder; 100 of 118 trials combined the drug with a non-drug treatment. These support the claim's closing sentence.

key_findings.correction: Figure 1 viewed: 111, 31 and 99 studies, and the ten exclusion reasons as listed in the sample field.
Note confirmed independently: I² 77.64%, 20 trials summing to 5931, Mason 2006 1.04 and Berger 2013 1.15. Berger 2013 is a US family-medicine trial (ref. 23).
Note confirmed independently: Figure 4 has 20 trials summing to 2719, which equals the any-dose 4604 minus 946 and 939; Figure 6 has 23 trials, I² 58.72%.
Figure 3 viewed, recalculation reproduced (DerSimonian-Laird): second control groups 1.03 (0.90-1.17), n 622; first control groups 0.94 (0.86-1.03); all five rows 0.99 (0.92-1.06), Q 4.90.
Figure 7 viewed: naltrexone withdrawals due to adverse events graded moderate for harm.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: the RR intervals imply about 7.8-18.9 (acamprosate), 9.7-126 (naltrexone, any drinking) and 7.5-20.9 (heavy drinking) at the implied baseline risks; with the figures' crude placebo rates I get the card's 10 (7-17), 21 (11-147) and 10 (7-19).
E.g. injectable naltrexone P = .14 equals Figure 4's Q(1) = 2.20, P = .14.

Found independently. My DerSimonian-Laird recomputation gives 0.99 (0.95-1.05) from the 7 placebo rows and 1.00 (0.96-1.04), Q 5.90, from all 11, which reproduces the figure. The 4 second rows also sum to exactly 1141, the head-to-head n, which supports the card's reading.
Found independently (5931; 20 trials and 2719; 19 trials and 2875).

Ref. 26 is Chick's naltrexone trial and ref. 27 his acamprosate UKMAS trial; Figure 2 cites 26 and Figure 6 cites 27. The placebo arm of 254/309 is shared between Figure 2 ('Anton 2005') and Figure 4 (Anton 2006, ref. 19).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low (items 4, 7, 11 and 15 no) is well argued from the article. Items 4 and 7 might be partly met in the AHRQ technical report, which neither reader read. Even then, items 11 and 15 alone would keep the rating critically low.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair: the conclusions follow the graded pooled estimates, and the problems are in the reporting (NNT intervals, counts, Figure 5).

missed: The Results text contradicts the gabapentin figure in the Table: it says gabapentin was not significantly associated with lower return to heavy drinking, while giving RR 0.90 (0.82-0.98), which excludes 1. The Table and Discussion count it as low-strength evidence of benefit (Results > Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 2nd paragraph). A reporting issue should record this, because claims cite the gabapentin result.

Support for reporting issue 2, and a usable figure: the four repeated rows of Figure 5 are the head-to-head contrasts (COMBINE 303+309, Kiefer 40+40, Morley 55+53, Mann 172+169 = 1141). So COMBINE supplies 612 of 1141 (53.6%) of the head-to-head heavy-drinking pool. The text does not state this share; it is derivable only from the figure.
